title: Remotes, Forks, and the Full Mental Model

questions.prompt: Your push is rejected as non-fast-forward. A colleague pushed first. What do you do?
options: git push --force, so your commit wins
git fetch origin, then merge or rebase origin/main, then push again
git push --force-with-lease, so your commit wins when the remote has not moved
git reset --hard origin/main, discarding your local commits, then push
questions.explanation: Non-fast-forward means the remote has commits you do not; the fix is to get them and then combine, in either direction you chose in Lesson 14. Forcing (A) deletes your colleague's commit — the exact failure that flag causes. `--force-with-lease` (C) still overwrites whenever the remote *hasn't* moved, which is precisely the case that just failed, so it would reject too. Hard-resetting to origin/main (D) throws away your own work to solve a problem you did not have.

options: The current state of main on the remote, queried live
Your local record of what main looked like on the remote at your last fetch, which can be stale
A branch on your machine that mirrors the remote automatically
A read-only view maintained by the hosting platform
questions.explanation: It updates only when you fetch — which is exactly why the non-fast-forward rejection in the sibling question could surprise you: your `main` matched a memory, not the server. Live state (A) would make that rejection impossible to encounter. It is a local ref (C), not a mirror kept in step. And it is a plain branch ref in your own repository (D), maintained by your fetch, not by the platform.

questions.prompt: You have no write access to a repository and want to propose a change. What is the path?
options: Request write access from the owner, then push directly to main
Fork it to your own account, push to your fork, and open a pull request against the original
Push to the original's main and open a pull request from your local machine
Email the maintainer a patch file generated from git format-patch
questions.explanation: Push access is the constraint, so the fork exists to give you somewhere you *can* push — then the pull request asks the original to take your commits. Pushing to the original (C) is rejected by definition. Waiting for write access (A) works but turns a five-minute contribution into a wait. A patch email (D) is a genuine 2005 workflow that no longer matches how anyone reviews code, and it is not what the lesson teaches.

questions.prompt: Before pushing a long-running feature branch to a shared repo, which one command tells you what you are about to publish?
questions.explanation: `origin/main..feature` is the set of commits you have that the remote does not — precisely the set a push would publish, and the set you should be able to defend line by line. `git status` (A) shows uncommitted work, which is a different question. `git branch -a` (C) lists labels, not commits. And `git diff` (D) shows the net tree difference, which can look empty or huge while hiding exactly the intermediate commits you did not mean to ship.
